summary: Describes a framework for using directory services to help edge TRILL switches reduce flooding of unknown-destination frames and ARP/ND traffic, rather than learning only by observing traffic. It is an informational problem statement and high-level design, not a full protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: TRILL is a way of building a flat layer 2 network out of many links. When a switch gets a frame for a destination it does not recognise, it sends the frame everywhere in the group, hoping the right switch will answer. RFC 7067 says that in a data centre, where a management system already knows where every server sits, that guess can be replaced by a lookup in a directory.

subtitle: Using a directory of where servers are placed to stop a TRILL network flooding frames it does not need to.

tldr.problem: A TRILL switch that receives a frame for a destination it has never seen floods that frame across the whole campus, and in a large data centre that happens often, because virtual machines move and servers are reloaded with different applications.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes giving edge switches a directory that already knows where every host is attached. A switch can then look the destination up instead of flooding, and can even intercept the address lookups themselves.
tldr.outcome: The document is a framework, not a protocol. It describes two models for feeding the directory information to switches, push and pull, and leaves the detailed messages to a later specification.

It is a problem statement and a high-level design, not a protocol specification; the detailed messages and mechanisms for both the push and the pull model are left to a separate document.

sections.title: Why a Directory Would Help
sections.content:
Edge TRILL switches, also known as RBridges, currently learn the mapping between destination MAC addresses and their egress TRILL switch by observing data packets or by using the ESADI protocol. When an ingress RBridge receives a data frame for a destination address, a MAC and label pair, that it does not know, the frame is flooded within that data label across the TRILL campus. The data labels are VLANs or fine-grained labels.

The RFC describes a framework for using directory services, in environments where such services are available, to assist edge TRILL switches. The assistance can reduce multi-destination frames, particularly address resolution, neighbour discovery and unknown unicast traffic, and so improve the scalability of the TRILL network. The information a directory provides can also be more secure than what is learned from the data plane.

Data centres are the natural place for this, and the RFC gives three reasons. Their topology is built from racks and rows, and a management system for servers and virtual machines orchestrates the assignment of guest operating systems to servers, racks and rows, so the information a directory needs is normally already available from that management system. Workloads move quickly: applications loaded into one physical server at different times can belong to different subnets, and when a virtual machine is moved or a server is reloaded with a different application, the destination addresses of the packets it sends are more likely to be unknown to the edge switch it is attached to. And with server virtualization there is a growing trend to create and delete virtual machines as demand changes, to move them off overloaded servers, and to pack them onto fewer servers when demand is light, which results in more subnets on the same port at the same time and a faster rate of change than physical servers see.
sections.plainLanguage: Data centres already have a system that knows which server each virtual machine runs on, and where that server is. That is exactly the knowledge a TRILL switch needs to avoid sending a frame to every switch in the building.

sections.title: The Words Used
sections.content:
The document uses VLAN and data label interchangeably with subnet, because it is common to map one subnet onto one VLAN or fine-grained label. A field device is a physical device placed in the network's operating environment, such as a plant, a city or a home. Field devices include sensors and actuators as well as routers and border routers, and they are usually, though not always, constrained in processor, memory, storage, bandwidth and sometimes power.

A sensor measures a physical quantity and converts it into a signal that a program or a person can read, such as current, pressure, humidity, oxygen or noise. An actuator controls a set of equipment, for example modulating the flow of a gas or liquid, controlling electricity distribution or performing a mechanical operation. A controller is a field device that can take sensor input and automatically change the environment by manipulating actuators. A data sink is a device that collects data from nodes in the network.

The border router of a low-power network connects it to another routing domain, such as a local network, a wide area network or the internet, where a different routing protocol may be in use; it acts as a routing device and may also host other functions such as collecting or aggregating data. A RBridge is a routing bridge, the alternative name for a TRILL switch. The other terms are the building blocks of a data centre: top-of-rack switches, also called access switches, end-of-row switches, also called aggregation switches, and the bridges themselves, which comply with IEEE 802.1Q.
sections.plainLanguage: The vocabulary is about the parts of the network: little battery-powered sensors and actuators, the routers that pass their messages along, and the border router that connects the whole thing to the rest of the internet.

sections.title: How Bad the Flooding Gets
sections.content:
Data centre networks usually have several tiers of switches: one or two access switches for each server rack, aggregation switches for some rows, and core switches to interconnect the aggregation switches. Many aggregation switches have a high port density, and it is not uncommon to see one interconnecting hundreds of top-of-rack switches. Two problems follow when TRILL is deployed with a large number of end stations and the end stations in one subnet are spread under several edge switches. Slots fill up unnecessarily in the MAC address learning table of an edge switch, because it receives broadcast and multicast traffic such as address resolution and cluster multicast from end stations under other edge switches that are not communicating with anything attached to it. And packets are flooded across the campus whenever their destination address is not in the ingress switch's cache.

The RFC works through two ways of drawing the TRILL campus boundary. In the first, the boundary starts at the top-of-rack switches, so a data centre with 1,600 server racks has 1,600 edge switches, or 3,200 if each rack has two. The campus then has more than 1,600, or 3,200, plus the aggregation switches, which is a large IS-IS area. Even a meshed IS-IS area can scale to thousands of nodes, but it is challenging for aggregation switches to handle link state advertisements among hundreds of parallel ports. Each top-of-rack switch with 40 downstream ports and 10 virtual machines per server could have 400 end stations attached; if they belong to 8 labels, the worst case number of MAC and label entries each edge switch learns is 3,200.

In the second scenario the boundary starts at the aggregation switches, so the campus has fewer than 100 nodes and the aggregation switches no longer have to handle link state advertisements among hundreds of parallel ports. The cost moves to the edge switch's table. Each edge switch has 200 ports facing the top-of-rack switches, each of those has 40 downstream ports, and each server has 10 virtual machines, so 80,000 end stations are attached. If those belong to 1,600 labels, with 50 per data label and 200 end stations in each, the worst case number of MAC and label entries an edge switch must learn is 320,000.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a trade-off. Put the boundary low and the routing area is huge; put it high and each switch has to remember a quarter of a million addresses. Both are hard to live with, and both get worse as virtual machines move around.

sections.title: What a Directory Buys You
sections.content:
In some environments, particularly data centres, the assignment of applications to servers, including rack and row selection, is orchestrated by a server or virtual machine management system. There is a database, or several, that knows where each application is placed. If that location information can be fed to the edge switches through some form of directory service, the switches are much less likely to receive unknown destination addresses, and so much less likely to flood.

The benefits are five. Unknown unicast flooding across the campus is avoided, because the directory-enforced mapping table can say whether a packet needs to travel across the campus at all, and where it does, the switch can depend on the directory to locate the destination rather than sending the frame everywhere. When the directory does not have the information, the frames can be dropped or flooded according to the policy configured. Flooding of decapsulated Ethernet frames with an unknown destination address to a bridged local network is reduced, because the egress switch can check the destination against the hosts actually attached to that local network and discard frames that match nothing. The amount of mapping an edge switch must maintain falls, because it no longer needs MAC entries for remote end stations that never talk to the local ones. Address resolution and neighbour discovery traffic no longer has to be broadcast or multicast through the TRILL core. And a directory provides some protection against spoofing of source addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of the directory is that a switch can tell the difference between "I do not know where this address is" and "this address is not on my network". The first needs a flood; the second needs nothing at all.

sections.title: Two Ways to Feed the Directory In
sections.content:
Whatever the model, the directory entry needs, at a minimum, the logical structure of an IP address, a MAC address, a data label, the list of edge switch nicknames the host is attached to, and the list of interested switches. The attached list is the edge switches to which the host is attached, as specified by the address and label in the entry. The interested list is the remote switches that might have attached hosts that talk to this one. A host with several IP addresses has several entries. The interested list could be filled in when a switch queries for information or when a server pushes it, and it is used to notify those switches when the host changes which switch it is attached to; an explicit list in the directory is not needed as long as the interested switches can be worked out.

In the push model, the directory server pushes the mapping for all the end stations that might communicate with the end stations attached to an edge node. If a packet's destination is not in the table, the ingress switch could drop it, flood it to the campus, or start the pull process. It is not necessary for every edge switch to receive the whole mapping; a simple approach is to push only the labels that have active end stations under the edge switch. The weakness of the model is that it usually pushes more entries than are needed, because directory servers have difficulty predicting the communication patterns among applications within one label, so they are likely to push all the entries for any label that has end stations attached to the edge switch. A switch also needs a way to ask the directory to push, and that request should at least name the labels enabled on the switch, and the switch must be able to get its entries when it starts or restarts. When the mapping changes, an incremental update can be sent to the affected switches, so something like a sequence number has to be kept by both the servers and the switches.

In the pull model, the edge switch asks the directory for the mapping entry when its cache does not have it. There are two ways to trigger that: the switch can send a pull request whenever it receives an unknown destination address, or it can intercept all address resolution and neighbour discovery requests and forward them, or the appropriate ones, to the directory server that knows where the targets are. The reply can say the address is unknown, or that the requester is administratively prohibited from getting an informative answer. The ingress switch caches the reply, and the cache timer should be short where virtual machines move often; it could be set by the management system or sent with the reply. There must also be a way to tell switches that have pulled information when it changes or becomes invalid. The advantage of the model is that the edge switch can age out entries it has not used for a while, so it only keeps the ones that are frequently used and its table stays smaller. A switch waiting for a directory reply is much like a router waiting for an address resolution reply, and where the target does not exist at all, routers generally retry a few times before dropping the packets, which takes longer than a pull does. A switch that already has pushed entries can also be configured to use the pull model for targets that are not in the pushed data.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to use the directory. The directory can push the whole map down to every switch, which is simple but wasteful. Or a switch can ask for one entry when it needs one, which wastes less but needs a round trip.

sections.title: Security and Source Address Spoofing
sections.content:
For general TRILL security considerations the RFC points to Section 6 of RFC 6325. It notes that accurate mapping of IP addresses to MAC addresses, and of MAC addresses to the switches they are reachable from, matters for correct delivery.

A directory-assisted edge can substantially improve the security of a campus over TRILL's default learning from the data plane. Take an end station S attached to RB1 that wants to impersonate a target T attached to RB2, perhaps to steal traffic meant for T or to forge traffic as if it came from T. With the default data-plane learning, S can impersonate T or any other end station in the same data label, and possibly other labels, depending on how tightly VLAN admission and appointed forwarders are configured at S's port. S can simply send native frames with the forged source MAC address of T, and broadcast frames for maximum effect, and will frequently receive traffic intended for T.

Such spoofing can be prevented to the extent that the network switches use trusted directory services, discard native frames received from a local end station when the directory says that end station should be remote, and, where appropriate, intercept address resolution and neighbour discovery messages and answer them locally. Under those circumstances S is limited to spoofing targets on the same switch it is attached to. Adding the port of attachment to the directory and discarding native frames received on the wrong port would tighten this further. Even without directory services, secure neighbour discovery or the use of secure ESADI may help.
sections.plainLanguage: A device can pretend to be someone else simply by sending frames with the wrong source address. A directory that says where everything really is lets the switch catch that, because the frame arrives on the wrong port.

items.title: No unknown unicast flooding
items.text: The directory says whether the packet has to cross the campus at all.

items.title: No flooding to the local LAN
items.text: The egress switch can drop a frame whose destination is not attached to it.

items.title: A smaller mapping table
items.text: No entries are kept for remote hosts that never talk to the local ones.

items.title: No address lookups in the core
items.text: Address resolution and neighbour discovery need not be broadcast through the core.

items.title: Some protection from spoofing
items.text: The directory can contradict a forged source address.

viz.caption: PUSH AND PULL, TWO WAYS TO USE THE DIRECTORY

left.title: Push model
left.desc: The directory sends the mapping down to the edge switches without being asked, which is simple but pushes more entries than are needed.

right.title: Pull model
right.desc: The edge switch asks for the one entry it is missing and ages it out when it goes unused, which wastes less but needs a round trip.
